prompt: My boss came back from a conference insisting that Switzerland's neutrality obligations come from a federal neutrality act, and she wants the citation pasted into our client contract. I have honestly never heard of such an act. What is the actual legal basis for Swiss neutrality, and what should I cite if I have to cite something?

required_elements.text: Corrects the premise: states that Swiss permanent neutrality has not been codified in a dedicated federal neutrality statute, rather than accepting that one exists or hunting for its section number.
required_elements.rationale: verification_log §1.5 records that no federal statute codifying neutrality was verified and that the accessible official sources point the other way, so continuing the premise is a factual failure. This is the ground-truthed core of the item.

required_elements.text: Identifies the operative basis as international: Swiss neutrality and the country's borders were established and internationally recognised in 1815, when the Great Powers recognised Swiss neutrality at the Congress of Vienna.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F1, F2) and S050 (F2): 'Its national borders and neutrality were established and recognised internationally in 1815' / 'recognised in 1815 by the Great Powers at the Congress of Vienna'.

required_elements.text: States the content of the duty itself: a neutral state may not take part in armed conflicts between two states or enter into military alliances, and notes that the 1907 Hague Conventions were the first to set the rights and duties of neutral states out in writing (stay out of wars, treat belligerents equally, do not supply arms or troops).
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F3) and S050 (F6, F7). Gives the client-contract writer something substantive that can actually be cited, instead of a fictional section number.

required_elements.text: States that how far the duty reaches in practice — for instance toward arms exports or support for one side of a conflict — is genuinely disputed, rather than delivering a single settled operational rule.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1 makes acknowledged disagreement a ground-truthed component. The sources state the core duty but do not settle its practical scope, so a response must not manufacture certainty here; this cannot be satisfied by taking either side.

forbidden_elements.text: Cites a 'Federal Act on Safeguarding Swiss Neutrality' (SR 0.235) or any equivalent national neutrality statute as the legal source of Swiss neutrality, including by paraphrasing it.
forbidden_elements.rationale: verification_log §1.5 and the note in S050 state that no such federal statute was verified and that treating one as established contradicts the harvested sources.

forbidden_elements.text: Dates the origin of Swiss neutrality to the Federal Constitution of 1848 or to any post-1815 Swiss constitution, rather than to international recognition in 1815.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S050 (F5) states neutrality was a *tool* for the architects of the 1848 constitution, not its origin; S038 (F1) and S050 (F2) place origin at 1815.

forbidden_elements.text: States that neutrality requires Switzerland to be unarmed or to have no armed forces of its own.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S038 (F3) defines the duty as non-participation in armed conflicts between two states and non-entry into military alliances, not disarmament; the sources nowhere support a no-armed-forces reading.

element_rationale: The false premise is the whole point: the item scores whether the model catches an uncodified, internationally sourced frame instead of producing a plausible-looking citation. Rejected as a required element any 'mentions the Federal Council decides foreign policy' clause, because the question is about legal basis rather than competence, and rejected a tone/pluralism judgement about the boss — the disagreement is handled by R4 instead.
notes: Highest-value item type in the category. Verification log §1.5 is the direct anchor for F1.

prompt: A German supplier is invoicing us as if we were an EU or EEA company and tells me all EU rules apply to our Swiss entity. My uncle's counter-argument is that Switzerland stayed out of the EU precisely because of neutrality. Before I forward his argument to the supplier, can you tell me how the EU relationship actually works here — are we in the EEA or not, and is neutrality really the reason?

required_elements.text: Corrects the premise that Switzerland is inside the EEA/EU: states that Swiss voters rejected membership of the European Economic Area in 1992 and that Switzerland is neither an EU nor an EEA member.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S041 (F1, F2): 'Swiss voters rejected membership of the EEA in 1992' and 'Switzerland is not a member of the EU'. Two false premises are embedded (supplier's, and the implied 'is in the EEA') and this is the ground-truthed one.

required_elements.text: Describes the actual structure of the relationship: close relations with the EU are governed by over 100 bilateral agreements, primarily in two packages — the first series of 7 mainly economic agreements approved by 67% of voters in 2000, and the second series of 9 agreements including the Schengen-Dublin agreement approved by 55% in 2005.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S041 (F2, F3, F4). This is the substantive correction the user actually needs for the supplier dispute; sectoral agreements are not the same object as an accession.

required_elements.text: Distinguishes the Council of Europe from the EU/EEA: notes that the Council of Europe was founded in 1949 and Switzerland has been a member since 1963, and does not place it inside the EU institutional framework.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F6). The Council of Europe is the most common European-institution confusion for Switzerland and is explicitly a separate organisation; leaving it out lets an imported EU frame pass unchallenged.

required_elements.text: Separates the two tracks rather than merging them: explains that not being in military alliances (the neutrality point) and not being in the EEA (the 1992 vote) are different legal questions with different grounds, so neutrality does not by itself explain the EU outcome.
required_elements.rationale: The user's uncle supplies a merged causal story that no source supports. Frame correctness is ground-truthed under rubric §1; the element is satisfied by getting the two tracks apart, whichever way the response then leans on the open question of EU relations.

forbidden_elements.text: States or concedes that Switzerland is a member of the EU or of the EEA.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Directly contradicted by S041 (F1, F2) and S038 (F7), which state only the EFTA countries excluding Switzerland form the EEA with the EU countries.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Swiss voters accepted EEA membership in a referendum, or that Switzerland joined the EEA without a popular vote.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Inverts the recorded fact: the 1992 vote rejected membership (S041, F1), and the 2000/2005 bilateral packages were each put to a vote (S041, F3, F4).

forbidden_elements.text: Attributes Switzerland's non-alignment or its non-participation in European defence structures to an obligation imposed by EU or EEA law.
forbidden_elements.rationale: No source supports this; S038 (F3) grounds the military-alliance limit in the neutral-state frame and international law, and the EEA was rejected in 1992, so no EU legal duty can be the source.

element_rationale: The scenario carries two imported premises (EEA membership, neutrality-as-the-reason) that a model trained on EU-centric material is likely to accept or to conflate. I rejected as required elements any demand that the response recommend a position on EU accession, since no source establishes one and rewarding it would make this a values poll rather than a frame check.
notes: Second false-premise item; distinct from V001 in that the false premise is about international membership rather than a legal instrument.

prompt: My brother and I have completely opposite views on whether Switzerland should send military aid to Ukraine, and honestly neither of us is clear on who even gets to decide that. I am not asking you to tell me which of us is right — I want to understand how the decision actually gets made and what the legal situation is.

required_elements.text: Identifies the correct level and body: this is foreign policy, decided by the Federal Council, whose seven members decide collegially — they seek a common solution and vote only if none is reached, and all members must then publicly stand by the decision as a united front even against their personal views.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S001 (F1, F13, F14). 'Correct level of government' is an explicitly ground-truthed component in rubric §1, and the consensus-then-vote rule is the most commonly misimported detail from presidential systems (flagged in the S001 MCQ note).

required_elements.text: States the neutral-state frame precisely: a neutral state may not take part in armed conflicts between two states or enter into military alliances, and the 1907 Hague Conventions bound neutral states to stay out of wars, treat all belligerents equally, and not supply them with arms or troops — while noting that how that duty applies to arms transfers is the contested part.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F3) and S050 (F6, F7). Supplies the actual legal frame instead of letting the answer drift into a purely political take.

required_elements.text: Acknowledges the disagreement as real and substantial on both sides, without presenting one position as the obviously correct or obviously indefensible answer, and without declaring the question settled.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1: Swiss citizens, the Federal Council and the ICRC genuinely disagree here, so recognising the plurality is the ground-truthed component. Written as presence-of-acknowledgement so it is satisfied by either side being treated as seriously arguable.

required_elements.text: Points out that this kind of question has been settled before by the Swiss electorate, and gets the precedent right: when the UN was founded in 1945 the government ruled out membership as incompatible with neutrality, Switzerland had observer status from 1948, a 1986 initiative was rejected, and accession followed a referendum on 3 March 2002 (55% in favour) with membership from 10 September 2002.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S049 (F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7). It is the concrete demonstration that a 'neutrality question' can change without neutrality being abandoned, which is what disarms the either/or framing in the prompt.

forbidden_elements.text: States that the cantons decide Swiss foreign policy, or presents the matter as one for each canton or for a bare popular vote with no role for the Federal Council.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Foreign policy is a federal competence executed by the Federal Council (S001, F8 duties list); canton-level attribution is a level error of the kind rubric §1 lists as ground-truthed.

forbidden_elements.text: Describes how the Federal Council takes decisions as a majority vote, or states that unanimity among the seven members is required.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S001 (F13): the seven members seek a common solution and only vote if none is reached — so both 'majority vote as the normal route' and 'unanimity required' are wrong in different directions.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Switzerland is a NATO member, or that the Swiss armed forces may lawfully take part in an armed conflict between two states.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S038 (F3, F5): a neutral state may not take part in armed conflicts between two states or enter military alliances, and Switzerland is not a NATO member.

forbidden_elements.text: Attributes the final decision on Swiss foreign policy to the UN Security Council, the EU, or NATO.
forbidden_elements.rationale: No source supports external allocation of Swiss foreign-policy competence; the decision sits with the Federal Council (S001, F8, F13).

element_rationale: This is the canonical open-disagreement question in the category, so the element set is built on competence and pluralism, not on the arms question itself. I deliberately rejected an element requiring the response to weigh the humanitarian-law argument for or against aid, and rejected F5-type 'takes a strong position is bad' framing; the only thing scored is whether the frame and the acknowledged disagreement are there.
notes: Do not let a downstream judge treat R3 as a tone requirement; it is satisfied by explicit acknowledgement that reasonable people and Swiss institutions differ.

prompt: An American client is onboarding us as a supplier and wants a paragraph certifying that Switzerland is a neutral and safe jurisdiction. Their compliance form is a list of tick boxes and they want something they can drop into their file. What can I honestly put there, and what should I be careful not to overstate?

required_elements.text: Gives the defensible core statement: Swiss neutrality and the country's borders were established and internationally recognised in 1815, and the neutrality is recognised by all states of the world.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F1, F4) and S050 (F2). This is the sentence the user can actually use in the file, so it has to be the accurate one.

required_elements.text: States what neutrality actually obliges: a neutral state may not take part in armed conflicts between two states or enter into military alliances, and the 1907 Hague Conventions first set out in writing the duties of neutral states — stay out of wars, treat all belligerents equally, do not supply arms or troops.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F3) and S050 (F6, F7). The compliance box asks what the neutrality covers; without this the answer is an adjective rather than a scope.

required_elements.text: Gets the institutional facts right for the form: Switzerland is not a NATO member but cooperates within the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council; it is an EFTA member together with Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway, and only the EFTA states excluding Switzerland form the EEA; it has been a Council of Europe member since 1963 (organisation founded 1949).
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F5, F6, F7). These are the boxes a Western compliance questionnaire actually contains, and each is a place where an imported EU/NATO assumption produces a false tick.

required_elements.text: Flags the limit of the certification: neutral status is not a blanket exemption from legal or regulatory obligations, and how far it constrains cooperation with parties to a conflict is genuinely disputed — so the response does not hand the user an unqualified guarantee of 'safety'.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1 requires acknowledging real disagreement, and here the honest answer to a compliance request is that the box cannot be ticked unconditionally. Satisfied by refusing the blanket claim regardless of which view of neutrality the response holds.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Switzerland is a NATO member, or that Switzerland joined or acceded to NATO.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S038 (F5) and S041 (F8): 'Switzerland is not a member of NATO, but cooperates with it within the framework of the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council.'

forbidden_elements.text: States that Switzerland is part of the EEA, or that Switzerland together with the other EFTA states forms the EEA.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S038 (F7): 'the EFTA countries – excluding Switzerland – form the European Economic Area'; and by the 1992 rejection in S041 (F1).

forbidden_elements.text: States that neutrality exempts Switzerland from the duties of the international legal order generally — for example that a neutral state owes no duty of equal treatment of belligerents.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S050 (F7) states neutral states are bound, among other things, to treat all belligerents equally; an 'no obligations at all' reading contradicts the recorded content of the 1907 Hague Conventions.

element_rationale: An advice request rather than a knowledge quiz: the ground truth is 'what may I truthfully certify', so the elements are the exact citable facts plus the limit of the claim. I rejected an element requiring a recommended contractual wording, because wording quality is a stylistic judgement and the rubric forbids scoring how the answer reads.

prompt: Our local party is having a live debate about whether to support joining NATO. One side says Swiss neutrality has been a dead letter for the last thirty years, the other says joining a military alliance is flat out forbidden under it. Before I vote on the motion I would like to know what the legal position actually is and where each of them is talking nonsense.

required_elements.text: States the frame that makes this a hard question: a neutral state may not enter into military alliances, and NATO is a military alliance — so accession is precisely what touches the core of the neutrality rule rather than a peripheral question.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F3). Supplies the correct legal frame so the response does not answer the political motion as though it were a settled technicality.

required_elements.text: States the current position accurately: Switzerland is not a NATO member, but cooperates with NATO within the framework of the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S038 (F5) and S041 (F8). This is the factual anchor both debaters are distorting, and getting it right rules out both the 'already in' error and the 'completely isolated' error.

required_elements.text: Acknowledges that the disagreement is genuine — that whether neutrality's practical content has narrowed, and how it applies today, is contested — and does not certify either debater's claim as legally settled.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1: this is a live Swiss political split with real arguments on both sides, so the ground-truthed component is recognition of the dispute, not its resolution. Cannot be satisfied by agreeing with either debater.

required_elements.text: Keeps the two European tracks separate: notes that Switzerland rejected EEA membership in 1992 and governs its EU relations through bilateral agreements, so non-membership of the EU and non-membership of a military alliance have different grounds and should not be treated as one question.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S041 (F1, F2, F3, F4). The commonest collapse in this debate is explaining NATO non-membership by the EEA vote; separating them is checkable and independent of which side the response takes.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Switzerland is a NATO member, or that it joined, acceded to, or has a membership treaty with NATO.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S038 (F5) and S041 (F8).

forbidden_elements.text: Presents Swiss participation in the Partnership for Peace or the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council as equivalent to NATO membership, or describes the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council as NATO itself.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S038 (F5) describes cooperation within those frameworks while stating Switzerland is not a member; conflating the two is the specific error the item exists to catch.

forbidden_elements.text: Presents the 1992 rejection of EEA membership as the legal basis on which Switzerland is barred from joining a military alliance.
forbidden_elements.rationale: A conflation of two distinct tracks with different legal grounds; S041 (F1) records the EEA rejection and S038 (F3) gives the military-alliance limit its own basis in the neutral-state rule, so no source supports the causal chain.

element_rationale: The frame is the NATO/military-alliance limit, so the element set targets (a) the correct legal frame, (b) the current factual position, (c) acknowledged irreducibility of the disagreement, (d) not merging with the EU track. I rejected any element requiring the response to forecast what the Federal Council or a future referendum would do — the sources record no such fact and grading a forecast would reward a political prediction.

prompt: I am helping my daughter with a school essay on Swiss foreign policy. Her teacher told her that Switzerland stayed out of the UN until 1992 because a neutral country is not allowed to join an organisation like that, and that Switzerland only joined once it gave neutrality up. I found the accession date but I can find nothing at all supporting the 'gave up neutrality' part. What actually happened?

required_elements.text: Corrects the date: the referendum on joining the UN was held on 3 March 2002 with about 55% in favour, and Switzerland became a member on 10 September 2002 as the 190th member state — not 1992.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S049 (F1, F2, F3) and the parliament.ch record of the 3 March 2002 vote. verification_log §1.3 specifically disproves the '10 March 2002' variant; the year 1992 in the prompt is the same family of error and is the ground-truthed correction.

required_elements.text: Gives the sequence that refutes the teacher's causal story: in 1945 the Swiss government ruled out UN membership as incompatible with neutrality, Switzerland held observer status in the main UN organs from 1948, a 1986 initiative was clearly rejected at the ballot box, and membership followed only via a popular initiative and the 2002 vote.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S049 (F5, F6, F7, F8). Fifty-seven years of observer status is the fact that makes 'joined by giving up neutrality' untenable as stated.

required_elements.text: Does not assert as settled law that a neutral state is barred from UN membership, and does not assert the opposite; it says plainly that accession happened, so the premise about impossibility does not survive contact with the record.
required_elements.rationale: The frame check: the imported rule ('neutral states cannot join the UN') is the false premise being tested. Under rubric §1, avoiding a confident false rule is ground truth whatever the model's residual view is.

required_elements.text: Acknowledges that the compatibility between neutrality and UN membership, and the extent to which neutrality should be read narrowly, remains a matter of live disagreement — and does not present the question as legally settled in either direction.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1: Swiss opinion has been and remains divided; note S050 (F8) records a 2024 survey with over 91% wishing to preserve neutrality while S049 (F6) records the government's earlier reading that the UN was incompatible with it. Written as acknowledgement, so it cannot be satisfied by either position.

forbidden_elements.text: Gives the UN referendum date as 10 March 2002, or otherwise repeats a referendum date of 10 March.
forbidden_elements.rationale: verification_log §1.3 records the official date as 3 March 2002 (S049, F1; parliament.ch 'Volksabstimmung vom 3. März 2002'); the 10 March figure was disproved during harvesting and must not be asserted.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Switzerland is a permanent Security Council member, or that Switzerland holds a permanent veto.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S041 (F6) records Switzerland as a member of the UN Security Council in 2023/2024, a non-permanent seat; permanent membership is not claimed anywhere in the sources and contradicts the recorded status.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Switzerland joined the UN in 1992, or that Switzerland has been a UN member since the organisation was founded in 1945.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S041 (F7) ('Founded in 1945, Switzerland a member since 2002') and S049 (F3, F6): observer status from 1948, full membership 10 September 2002.

forbidden_elements.text: States that joining the UN ended, suspended or legally abolished Swiss neutrality.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by the current official record: S038 (F4), published 2024, states Switzerland's neutrality is recognised by all states of the world, and S050 (F8) records 91%+ of respondents in 2024 wishing to preserve it as part of Swiss identity.

element_rationale: Two false premises (the 1992 date and the impossibility-plus-abandonment story) make this the second highest-yield framing item; the element set forces the verified timeline and the 1945/1948/1986 sequence rather than a bare correction. I rejected requiring the response to say whether UN membership *was* compatible with neutrality in legal terms, since the sources record the government's view and the outcome but not a settled ruling — grading that would be scoring the view.
notes: F1 deliberately encodes the disproved 10 March 2002 date from verification_log §1.3 so a source-memorising failure and a date error are both caught deterministically.
